utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton, legal intern Marija Knezevic, case manager Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with Negosava Smiljanic, case manager, and Jolana Makraiova, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, good morning. The first questions I'm going to put to you will concern your yesterday's evidence. There are some things that need to be clarified. Once again, I will ask you to speak slowly when answering my questions. On page 9323, line 18, it says that you saw a list of the population in Pacetin. That list dates back to 1990. And according to that list, Pacetin had 1100 inhabitants of whom 100 were Orthodox Roma and 1.000 Orthodox Serbs. Please look at the year, the year is 1990. Is that year correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. This is a big mistake. That was the 1900 or 1903 census --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. We have a technical problem, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Please continue, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, this is a big mistake. I suppose it is due to the interpretation or perhaps I spoke too fast, and the blame lies on me. That census was made over 100 years ago, and at that time the population was 100 per cent Orthodox, of them 11 per cent were Roma. They were all killed in 1941 and there are no longer any Roma in Pacetin. Maybe it will be interesting for the Trial Chamber that there are currently, 650 to 700 people living in Pacetin, which means over a period of 100 years, the population has been reduced by 50 per cent. A lot of the people were killed in the Second World War. All of the Roma were killed, and some 30 per cent of the Serbs were killed in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would also like to clarify another detail which concerns a question that I put to you yesterday about poetry and your attitude towards poetry. This is on page 9034, line 5. You said that you sometimes read poetry with a girlfriend but never with a man or a male friend. You said that you also accompanied your friend Branko Kovacevic to a poetry reading evening. That was before the war. Did you go somewhere where poetry was read, or did you go somewhere else? What was it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say when you asked me about reading or writing poetry, I have to say that I never wrote poetry. When I read poetry, since I graduated from grammar school and a grammar school gives a broader education, I did read poetry when I attended secondary school.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Hadzic please be reminded to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, please slow down when you speak. It is very difficult for the interpreters to follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you -- is it okay? Okay. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to make an impression that I did not like poetry. I did read poetry. I read well-known poets like Yesenin, Lorca, to mention but a few. As a result of having been grammar school student, I also read Croatian poets, Vujovic, Matos, but I never read amateur poetry, nor did I ever follow any friend's work or did it with a friend as a witness said. When it comes to attending that poetry reading evening, I went with my wife at the invitation of my friend Branko Kovacevic to his book presentation. I didn't go with Branko. Branko was the host who had invited us. That was a few years before the war, perhaps five or six years before the war. And, at that time, I still didn't sport a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 9337, line 8, you said that the SDP lost the elections in Croatia. Could you please tell us in a bit more detail what did you mean when you say they lost? Did they win any seats in the Croatian parliament at all? What did you mean when you say that they lost?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that the HDZ won, i.e., that it got a majority in the Croatian parliament. The SDP was the second-most powerful party in Croatia. It had fewer MPs than the HDZ, but it did win in many municipalities in Croatia, including Vukovar, where the SDP was the victorious party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let us look at two more pages, 9337 and 9338. That question concerned a debate in the Vukovar municipality with regard to the constitution and amendments to the constitutions and things like that. Let me ask you this: Did you have in mind the Croatian constitution according to which the Serbs would no longer be a constituent people or did you have another constitution in mind?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another constitution. The constitution that portrayed Croatia as an independent state. That's how we perceived it. We called it the so-called separatist constitution. All of us who were on the SDP list in our -- part of our platform was that we wanted Croatia to stay in Yugoslavia. That is the message that we sent to the people. I don't know when that happened. I know that it was in 1990. I can't even give you the month. Most of the Croatian MPs, SDP members, opted for that constitution, were in favour of that constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: You spoke about your contribution at a meeting in the Municipal Assembly. Did that debate take place before that constitution which you have just called a separate constitution was adopted?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure. I know it was adopted by the parliament and that all the municipal assemblies were supposed to adopt it as well. Or whether it was the other way around. In any case, the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar adopted that constitution but it also proposed very important amendments. That was never publicised anywhere. The only thing that we could read in the papers was: Well, there you go, even Vukovar has adopted that new constitution. That was the message in the press. I can't remember whether that comprised Slavica Bajan's [phoen] proposal that Serbs should be eliminated from the constitution or was it an entirely new version of the constitution. I can't remember, as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that you're not a legal professional, you're not a lawyer, and you cannot discuss any amendments, but you did mention amendments and we know that a municipality cannot adopt a state's constitution. When it comes to those amendments, did they mean that the constitutional proposal could be changed with those amendments. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand you. That was the gist of the whole thing. A majority of us didn't have anything against the Croatian constitution, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, something --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zivanovic switch his microphone off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My microphone is ... on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, I think now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Well, the question and then the answer have long since gone into the record, but, Your Honour, we will be objecting to leading questions and the objection would have been that the last question from my learned friend was a leading question. Because they both speak the language, Mr. Hadzic answered the question before I could raise the objection, but I did want to note that we are watching for leading questions and will object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I rephrase the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me, please, in view of your previous answer, and you have partially answered my previous question, what was the subject of debate at that Assembly meeting in Vukovar? What was your proposal and what was the proposal of those who were in favour of amendments?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, a high percentage of us supported the constitution of our republic, the Croatian constitution. However, I and some other Serbs, not a majority of the Serbs, also supported the amendment that was supposed to alter 1 per cent of the constitution, and that concerned Croatia staying in Yugoslavia and not being an independent state. That should have been a public proposal, and together with that amendment, we voted in favour of the constitution. I was against, all the other Serbs were in favour, fully confident that that amendment would be adopted. But it never happened. To be honest, only one other MP voted together with me against. All the other -- all the SDP and HDZ MPs were in favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This means in -- effectively that they were in favour of Croatia seceding from Yugoslavia. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not. Some of the HDZ MPs and the other parties were in favour of what you just said, but the party that I belonged to was in favour of the 90 per cent of the constitution and the amendment that would change that one bit. I thought that that amendment was pointless, that we should not vote in favour of that constitution, that we should turn it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to read one part of the minutes because, honestly, I didn't understand what exactly you said in that part of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zivanovic repeat the number of the page in the transcript and the number of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 9343, line 13. [In English] "Also there were some messages that had to do with specific things related to liquidations and we heard what was said by the TO and also arming Spegelj, et cetera, but all of this was before the arming."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please shed some light on this? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that mistake in the transcript, but it was -- it is not up to me to correct that. I believe that this will be corrected when they listen to the tape. Instead of TV they recorded my words as TO. I meant TV, meaning television, when the news was about Spegelj and arming which was a notorious fact. But instead of the abbreviation TV, the abbreviation that was recorded was TO. And if that is changed, I suppose that the situation will be a bit clearer, but if it's not I can explain.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the counsel please make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, since we're talking about that, can you please explain.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as these quiet liquidations are concerned, I heard about it for the first time on TV. Unofficially stories circulated among the Serbs that something was being planned, but that was the first time it was publicly confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly how it was confirmed on TV by Mr. Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us saw it. Everybody can still see it. It's the famous footage where Spegelj dispenses advice on how to settle scores with Yugoslav officers but also all those who support Yugoslavia, to come to a house and when the owner opens the door to fire two bullets in his stomach. And that story reminded me of the scenario from 1971, when the nationalist movement in Croatia was raging. I was a young student by now -- at that time. They also at that time distributed weapons among their supporters and also gave them postmen's uniforms, and the same instructions. Tudjman himself went to prison because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to this topic later. But now I should like to look at document P70.50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 70 -- [Interpretation] 70.50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have seen this text. It has been shown before during the trial, and this story mentions your name, among others, in the context of a peaceful protest in Vukovar. Do you remember this event?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This text says that you read a proclamation to the leadership regarding the police, asking that the police not protect you anymore. My first question is: Did you indeed read such a proclamation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a speech at the time to the people gathered, and there were several thousand, and I remember the atmosphere was very tense because we were surrounded by the special police with crowd-control equipment, with dogs, et cetera, and nobody dared come close to me because the usual thing is for somebody to announce the speaker and the programme, et cetera, so I had to read the agenda, the programme, myself so maybe the journalists understood that as a proclamation. I can't remember the details anymore. But what I said is that we don't need so many policemen with rifles in Vukovar. I didn't know who they were protecting and I didn't know why they had arrived. In fact they were not policemen. They were later to become their new army, but at that time I didn't know it. And by that time we had already been stricken out of the Croatian constitution, we, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This text also says that you had some comments to make on the Croatian constitution. It's in the second column on the -- on this page.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's true, that's what I said. And that was the thinking shared by most Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the Vukovar board of the Serb Democratic Party took place? Can you describe it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. After the second round of elections in Croatia, when, as I said before, the HDZ won and the SDP lost - it didn't disappear, it just lost, meaning that it had to two or three deputies less - I realised that nobody was protecting Serb interests anymore. Both the HDZ and the other pro-Croatian parties that were in coalition with the HDZ. And when I say "pro-Croat" I don't mean anything bad, it was just a fact. The SDP was supposed to represent the Serbs but it was too busy promoting its own interests so that nobody represented the interests of the Serbian people. Then at the initiative of four or five of us we went to Knin to meet with Professor Raskovic, in the month of May sometime, mid-May, I think, and we asked if he would agree that we establish the Serbian Democratic Party in the municipality of Vukovar because both Vukovar and Knin were in Croatia. He agreed and we scheduled a founding Assembly meeting for the 10th of June in Vukovar, in a place close to Vukovar. We did that, and then followed the technical aspects that I can describe later, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was later done to establish this board after this talk you had with Professor Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I skipped a very important thing. Just after we returned from Knin, we formed a so-called initiative board and named the chairman. He was my colleague from Vupik, now late Slobodan Tripic. We were 15 on that board, and we organised this founding Assembly in Vukovar for the 10th of April [as interpreted]. We organised security for the meeting. We obtained a permit for this meeting from the police, and we had talks in various local communes. We advertised it so that people would come and listen to Professor Jovan Raskovic, member of the academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat when the Assembly was to take place? I don't think the date we have on the LiveNote is correct.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the founding Assembly was held on the 10th of June, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this first contact with Professor Raskovic, what impression did he make on you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first impression was later confirmed when I got to know him better. He was one of the smartest people I've ever met. The impression he left was of a very composed, reasonable man, and his work later proved that he was, indeed, a calm, reasonable man promoting peace, completely contrary to the Dinarian type of person in the Balkans who are mostly impulsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in Knin, did you meet anyone else from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Marko Dobrijevic who was a lawyer in Knin. He had some technical job assisting Professor Raskovic and later Milan Babic, who was president of the Knin municipality. But I didn't talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before this rally on the 10th of June, could you tell us where this rally was to take place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to take place, and it was held, in Adica, which is a picnic place in the town of Vukovar. Perhaps 300 metres from the house of Mr. Boro Savic, at the end of his street.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was going on at that meeting, if you could tell us briefly. Who attended, were there any speakers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the main -- the keynote speaker was Professor Raskovic. There were other speakers from Knin, I believe, including Branko Popovic, who maybe attended some later rallies, so I might be confused about him. Also Slobodan Tripic addressed the people as chairman of the initiative board and Mr. Milan Paroski also spoke. I don't know who invited him but he introduced himself as an MP from Serbia. I don't know whether that was true. And I gave a very short speech. In fact, I only thanked the people for electing me as chairman of the Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you come to be elected president or chairman of the Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was nominated by the 15 people who were members of the initiative board who had met perhaps five or six times before this founding Assembly. In fact, they had to talk me into it because when I became a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, it didn't cross my mind that I could one day become a high-ranking official. Maybe I can tell you a story to describe the situation. When I returned home after being elected president, my father, who was by that time old and much wiser than I, when everybody was congratulating me, my father didn't. Instead he asked me what my salary would be. I thought that he didn't know anything about these things so I said: This is a honorary position. I'm just supposed to work. There's no salary. And my father said: Well, that's precisely why they elected you. If it were a good job, they would have taken someone else. They know that you will work for free. That's what I will always remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did Professor Raskovic ever make clear what his position was concerning the Serbs in Croatia and their position, whether they should stay within Yugoslavia, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was said so many times at many rallies: Serbs will stay in Croatia to the extent that Croatia stays in Yugoslavia. That was the main thing. And he always mentioned in all his speeches that from the times of Ante Starcevic, Serbs had been called disruptive, a disruptive factor in Croatia, which, of course, wasn't correct, and he explained why it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just -- if could you add something to your previous answer, when you said you were elected president of the Municipal Board. Which municipality was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Vukovar, within the boundaries of the municipality of Vukovar as per Croatian law that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You will recall that Boro Savic was heard by this Court. Can you tell -- tell us, since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've -- had known him perhaps for ten or 12 years before the war, which means from 1977 or 1978 or 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you come to know him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro was born in Sabac, Serbia. He was some sort of travelling salesman. He didn't have a serious job. He was married to a teacher from my village, who was a friend of mine and my then-girlfriend. And that woman teacher had a small studio, and Boro, when he came to visit, he stayed at her place because he didn't have an apartment. And later they got married and moved to Vukovar. I mean, Boro came to Pacetin almost as a homeless person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you say, I mean, well, how often did you see him? How did this go, this acquaintance of yours, or socialising, if we can call it that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before all of these things happened in relation to the SDS we did not really socialise. He is a considerably older than I am, and he had a different circle of friends. Perhaps -- well, that's characteristic. He did not make friends with people that he could not take advantage of, so I was not really part of his circle. So we had these relations within the party for about a year, from mid-May 1990 until 1991 mid-May, or, rather, last time -- actually the last time I saw him was around the 1st of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ou say that the last time you saw him was around the 1st of June, 1991. Can you remember what the situation was when you actually saw him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. It was at Vukasin Soskocanin's funeral in the village. And I think that after that I saw him only once before the war, during those ten days or so during the month of June or perhaps not even that. And then I only saw him in 1995 or 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the person whose funeral it was when you saw -- well, actually, you don't have to, because it's been corrected. I mean ... Now I'd like to ask you to take a look at the statement that you gave to the Prosecution. That is P50. It has to do with paragraph 7. You see, in paragraph 7, it says that he made you president of the board; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not correct. I was selected by the initiative board, and I said there were about 15 members there, and everybody was in favour, and Boro Savic was among those 15 who were in favour. So his participation was just one-fifteenth, like the remaining 14 persons, so this is a strange way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on he says that he was secretary of the SDS in Vukovar and that he wanted to appoint serious people. Can you say when it was that he was appointed secretary of the SDS for Vukovar, if that actually did happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he was appointed on the 10th of June, when I was selected, but I'm certain that he could not have been selected before that because the SDS did not exist before that in Vukovar. So what he said here is mind-boggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he a person who made appointments at all? As he put it here, he appointed these people to the board, or was it a body of the party that did that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said that he was secretary, and that office speaks in itself, how powerful he was. Let me be as mild as possible and as a fair as possible. He was an equal member. He was not inferior but he was not dominant either. We were all on a footing of equality but I cannot define it now. It was after Plitvice, after his suffering there, and I'm not sure that he -- well, this is a kind of egocentrism. I did not really know him to be that way before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question: He says that at the time there was this big problem, namely, the Socialist Party of Serbia of Slobodan Milosevic, as they considered that there should not be any other political party apart from the SPS [Realtime transcript read in error "SBS"]. At the time were you confronted with that problem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we will be talking about his entire statement now for a while, if I understand you correctly, I really feel ashamed because I used to work with Boro. I have to deny all of that and say that all of this is crazy. A normal person cannot be saying all of these things. It is crazy. What kind of influence did the Socialist Party have in the 1990s at Croatia. The SPS appeared only when the Krajina was established. He completely confused things here. And there's no chronological logic involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, a clarification in the transcript. At line 23 of the current page, it is said -- the acronym there is said to be SBS. And in line 5 -- well, no, 23 is the previous page. Line 5 of the -- of the actual page there is an acronym missing. Could you clarify that with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat once again the acronym of this political party. Or, rather, could you repeat what you said -- or actually I'm going to repeat the question to you because it actually has to do with my question. So my question was: It actually has to do with paragraph 7 of the statement, where it says that a special problem at the time was the Socialist Party of Serbia, abbreviated as SPS, the party of Slobodan Milosevic. Because they believed, allegedly, that only the SPS should exist there in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that was crazy. The SPS, this party of Slobodan Milosevic, did not appear there in any form during 1990. It was Croatia at the time. So not a single party from Serbia was there except for some of these opposition MPs from Serbia who came there, that's a very well-known thing, but the Serb authorities did not come at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8, he claims that the Party for Democratic Change of Ivica Racan, the SPD, won only a few seats. Can you tell us whether that is correct that this party, the SDP, had only a few seats?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct either. He said that in just a silly way, a stupid way. The SDP had many MPs, and in the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar they had an absolute majority of assemblymen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "many MPs," what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the parliament of Croatia, I mean the SDP. I'm just saying that in accordance with what he said here, several, a few. You can either say 50 or 70 or 30 and then everybody can conclude what is a lot or many, in relation to 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at paragraph 11. It says that a meeting was held of the Serb Democratic Party in August 1990 and that he could not attend and that the party split at that meeting. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not the truth. These are conclusions -- well, when I read this entire paragraph 11, I see that those who support conspiracy theories would be envious of these conclusions of his because this is simple fantasizing, not based in reality at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why you saying that this is fantasizing, that in August 1990 the SDS split or fell apart?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the SDS was established on the 17th of February, 1990. So from February to August, it is, what, six months, and it was only then that they had gained momentum and that they started operating, so they were getting stronger and stronger rather than falling apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that manifested in some way at the time, in that period, August 1990?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Vukovar we only started organising local boards and rallies, and Professor Raskovic appeared at some of them, so we were in full sway. He confused everything that happened there. After two or three years, all of this got mixed up in his head. I mean, I assume that this was needed for some other testimony so then it was just inserted by way of some compilation because this is totally senseless. It makes no sense whatsoever to say all of this. It never existed, these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which names?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The influence of Jovica Stanisic in 1990 over Milan Babic. That is totally impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm interested in here. Another thing that he mentioned. That Raskovic -- or, rather, that Raskovic warned him that the party would fall apart and that he specifically gave tasks to you and Vukcevic, Vojislav Vukcevic. Can you tell us whether that happened, did he give you some assignments, tasks, or to Professor Vukcevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borivoje Savic was secretary of the Municipal Board and I was president of that board, and he never gave me any assignments whatsoever. Now the Trial Chamber can take my word for it. I'm speaking under oath. But as far as Professor Vukcevic is concerned, I don't want to say now whether Boro gave assignments to him, but let me say that Professor Vukcevic was a doctor of law and for a while he was also the dean of the law school in Osijek and also he was a judge in Beli Manastir. He is at least 15 years older and at least three times smarter than Boro Savic, and Boro Savic could not give him any kind of assignment, ever, whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can move on to paragraph 22. Here, he says that he worked with his father in Vupik -- with your father in Vupik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father did work in Vupik, and after that, I worked there. I'm not sure whether Boro got a job in Vupik before I did. I think that I got a job before he did, but that doesn't matter. We worked together in Vupik, but we were not in the same basic organisation, so I did not really co-operate with him through our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says that sometime in mid-May he called you and told you that a board for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem would be set up. Can you see that? Did he really tell you that a board would be set up for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that. He could not tell me that at the time because that didn't exist at the time. Maybe this was written unbeknownst to him or he is totally insane; I mean, Boro Savic. These are some elementary things. It's like two plus two. There's nothing for me to prove. There is nothing for me to say about some things that did happen and cannot be changed, some things that are so obvious. I apologise. We first established the Municipal Board of the SDS in Vukovar. And then Municipal Boards were established in all the municipalities in Eastern Slavonia, meaning, Osijek, Beli Manastir, and Vinkovci. When it comes to Western Slavonia, Municipal Boards were set up in parallel with us, in Podravska Slatina a day before Vukovar and then in other places, and we did not take part in all that because the distance from us was about 200 kilometres. It was only towards the end of 1990 or the beginning of 1991, at the initiative of Ilija Sasic, Veljko Dzakula, myself, and Boro Savic that the Regional Board for Slavonia and Baranja was eventually established. And the term "Western Srem" did not appear before 1991. That term did not exist. I really could not talk to Boro. However, since I've known him, this is not the way he was. This is just a lot of nonsense. Whatever he knew, he merged together and told the story as if everything happened in 1991, but it didn't. Some things happened in 1992 and 1993. He mentions the Executive Board here. I believe that what he had in mind was the initiative board. I don't -- I can't read his mind. However, what I'm reading here is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you at least clarify this part because the Executive Board is mentioned here as well as the Regional Board. Could you please tell us which bodies or which organs did the Serbian Democratic Party have?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party was established in Knin on the 17th of February. It had its Main Board and its Executive Board, independently of Goran Hadzic and Boro Savic. At the time we did not even hear of the SDS. At least I didn't and I'm sure Boro didn't either. It was only in May that we started setting up our Municipal Board. We established the initiative board, and then on the 10th of June, the Municipal Board was set up. Before that, there was nothing. From then on we started setting up local boards in local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, you mentioned the Main Board of the SDS and the Executive Board. Which body had the supremacy, which was the highest party body?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The highest party body was the Main Board and its president was Jovan Raskovic. At the time I was not a party member. I don't know when the Executive Board was established. There was no need for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was it who set up the Executive Board, i.e., who selected the Executive Board members?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way things were done when I joined, it was the Main Board who did that. In politics, in the executive and judiciary power, you have to imagine the Main Board as the Assembly and the Executive Board as the government of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we're talking about the Executive Board, were you elected? Did you have a position in the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party? Specifically you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the party statute, every president of any Municipal Board automatically becomes a member of the Main Board. And later, as a member of the Main Board, I was elected as a member of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now tell me, it says here that you were the president of the Regional Board in the same paragraph, 22. Were you, indeed, the president of a Regional Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. The president of the Regional Board of the SDS for Slavonia was Veljko Dzakula, for Slavonia and Baranja only because Western Srem did not feature at the time. That term was coined by Ilija Petrovic. I don't know why. But it was only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And who were the members of that Regional Board? Were they elected, or were people just appointed based on their positions and functions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were presidents of Municipal Boards that -- and by virtue of those positions in Slavonia and Baranja, they became members of the Regional Board. And there was also Boro Savic as the secretary. This means that every Municipal Board could put forth another candidate in addition to their president.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He says that he was the one who helped you become a member of the Main Board of the SDS; is that correct? That's in paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I have to explain to this Honourable Trial Chamber, that, at that time, in the Republic of Croatia where we were, there were no candidates who would wholeheartedly accept any of the positions that involved such activities, so nobody needed to push anybody. We had a major problem to get members, to activate our membership. Nobody was overly ambitious to hold a position because that was all without any pay, as I just told you when I told you the story about my father. We only spent money because we used our cars, we bought our own petrol. Nobody actually paid us expenses. We -- as a result of our positions, we were out of our pockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 28. He says that he established the SDS board in Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. He says that that happened on the 9th of June, and that's also not correct. He is so off here. And, again, he mixes up things, and he uses a wrong chronology. He mentioned Slobodan Milosevic. At that time, a majority of the SDS members were against Slobodan Milosevic's policies and against the Serbian policies. It was a public matter. He is talking with hindsight and distorting things while doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 29, he mentions Ilija Petrovic and Ilija Koncarevic as well as Milan Paroski. He says that Koncarevic and Petrovic turned up as SDS activists from Vojvodina, although that party had not been set up there yet. Do you know if the Serbian Democratic Party was established in Serbia at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was established and registered in Serbia as the Serbian Democratic Party. But it was independent from its counterpart in Croatia. Boro Savic and I were even invited as guests to a founding meeting in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Ilija Koncarevic and Ilija Petrovic were members of that party, the Serbian Democratic Party, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Boro and I knew that because we were [as interpreted] our hosts there. They were party members, and we were their guests. That meeting took place in Novi Sad, and I believe that Professor Raskovic also attended. I'm not sure, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Paroski is also mentioned here in the same paragraph, paragraph 29, together with Koncarevic and Petrovic. He says that they put pressure on the SDS board in Vukovar. Are you aware of any pressure that was put on you to bear by Paroski or Koncarevic and Petrovic? And when I say "you," I mean your board in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither I know that nor was that possible, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately on the following page and the paragraph actually continues on that page, he says that -- or, rather, only Koncarevic and Petrovic said that they were representatives of the state security of Serbia and that they also represented President Milosevic. Did Koncarevic and Petrovic ever tell you any such thing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they never said that to me. And it's not correct. Boro is just making things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they hear them say that to somebody else or did you hear from somebody else --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard that. They were members of the Serbian Democratic Party for Serbia which means that could not be members of any service or delegates representing a president who had his own party. They were members of an entirely different party, so this just doesn't make sense. The Serbian Democratic Party in Serbia was an opposition party. It had its goals, and one of them was to take over power from the ruling party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was an opposition party to what party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SPS party, Milosevic's SPS, which was the ruling party at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, what was Ilija Koncarevic's position what was his profession? What did he do at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Koncarevic was a pensioner. He was pensioned off as captain first class in the JNA. And Ilija Petrovic, when I met him, he was introduced to me as the director of the postal services in Novi Sad. However, when I got to know him better, I realised that he was one of the junior managers in the postal service, so he was not the general manager of the whole postal service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's move to paragraph 35. You will find it in the middle of that paragraph. It says there that a majority of Serbs in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem shared his opinion that the Serbs should stay in Croatia. Can you comment upon that, if you understand what he meant?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the paragraphs that we have been discussing are just nonsensical. I can't say anything about the end of the paragraph before I say something about the beginning. He says that Raskovic listened to Milosevic. Everybody in Serbia knew that Raskovic was friends with Dobrica Cosic and that they -- their views were very opposite. And when he says that Raskovic became a MP because Milosevic wanted him to do that, but it's impossible. This -- these are all stupidities. They have nothing whatsoever to do with reality. All members of the Serb Democratic Party in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem supported Professor Raskovic's position and that position was Serbs will stay in Croatia to the extent Croatia stays in Yugoslavia. These positions by Raskovic were positions that he adopted after the peaceful reintegration. He seems to be defending himself here, although he was never charged with any crimes, either by this Tribunal or anywhere in Croatia. He says a majority of the Serbs. We had referendums, and 99.99 per cent of the Serbs were in favour of the opposite. These are elementary truths and it can be mathematically proven. He lives in Croatia now. He wants to curry favour with Croats that's why he is saying all these things which are not just lies but pure fantasies. Because when somebody has an ill-intent and lies, then he can do it and it cannot be proven. And he is lying about things that are so easily proven because they are notorious and everybody is aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think some parts of your answer are again missing from the record because you are speaking much too fast. When you said it was impossible that Dr. Raskovic rejected the offer to be an MP in the Croatian Assembly, Croatian parliament, why was it impossible that he did that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that it was impossible the way Boro Savic explained it, that Raskovic refused to be a member of the Croatian parliament because of pressure from Slobodan Milosevic. I'm not saying that he didn't have his own reasons, but he certainly didn't refuse it under pressure from Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Raskovic an MP in the Croatian parliament, ever?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to anticipate what Boro Savic was thinking. It seems to me implausible that my own associate would talk such rubbish. I suppose that he meant one of those five deputies who were elected on the SDS ticket, but the way he explained it is completely implausible. It's beyond understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of this paragraph, he says that the chequer-board emblem was also on the coat of arms of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. Can you tell us now, because the chequer-board emblem was mentioned many times as something that provoked the Serbs' discontent, could you tell us why it was disturbing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Boro said is true but he didn't invent hot water. We all know that. The chequer-board emblem existed since the Kingdom of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs, and it was also in the coat of arms of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, together with the four letters S. That's not in dispute. But the Serbs would not accept the chequer-board emblem as a separate symbol placed on the flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what does the chequer-board emblem consist of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has 25 fields, five by five, and in our documents while we were in the republic of Croatia, the first field was red, the following one white. During the independent state of Croatia, the first field in the left top corner was white so that a letter U could be placed in it, and the U meant Ustasha. And that's why the Serbs rejected the chequer-board emblem at that time. As for me personally, in my position, Boro did not say anything new here. I agree with it. Yes, the chequer-board symbol was on every document of mine - my school diploma, my other documents - but that's a completely different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we clear up another thing about this chequer-board. You say that in your documents, in fact, the documents issued by the Socialist Republic of Croatia, the first field was red, whereas in World War II the first field was white. Now, when the chequer-board emblem was to be reintroduced, how was it supposed to be introduced again? With the first field red or white?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say under oath that I'm sure, and perhaps I shouldn't speculate. But I suppose this is just the technical detail. The chequer-board emblem should not have caused a war. It shouldn't have been such a problem to Serbs, and I also blamed myself -- I blame myself now that I took it that way at the time. It's perhaps the legacy of Communism that it was so unacceptable to us. That's the only thing I can say I'm sure of under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move to paragraph 69. I don't need to show you this text because you probably remember this article from the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, as this is a new paragraph you are discussing now, would this be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take the break. Be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, could we now look at paragraph 69 of this statement. Would you please at paragraph 69 of the statement we've been reviewing.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this passage, Mr. Savic discussed an article published after you were released from prison, both of you, following your arrest at Plitvice, and he says that you were keen on accumulating, amassing various positions in the SDS party. Was that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. I had only one position: President of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. And under the statute of the Main Board of the party, that was a position that implied certain functions, regardless of who occupied it, and I was deputy to the Regional Board. What's interesting here is that Boro Savic was actually a member of every body that I was a member of. That's really curious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He says the same journalist wrote, and Boro Savic agrees, that Boro Savic was the SDS ideologist, a very knowledgeable one. Do you share this opinion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Boro Savic and I happened to be in Plitvice completely by chance, and it was by chance that we became public figures. Boro Savic was not the party ideologist. The main person in the party was Dr. Raskovic. And we came into the public eye quite by chance after Plitvice. Boro Savic was completely unknown to people. His speeches were never heard in public. People couldn't know him. I don't know what this journalist meant until -- unless he had parapsychological powers. Maybe he could read Boro Savic's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But to the best of your knowledge, was he really a knowledgeable ideologist of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not. He was not even very well educated. He said himself he had graduated from the secondary school of agriculture in Sabac and some higher school in Vinkovci. He didn't have the kind of education that would enable him to be an ideologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 70 of his statement. It relates to the day when both of you were released from the remand prison. And he said you were allowed to make a phone call then, and you phoned Ilija Koncarevic, whereas he had believed you would call your father. Can you recall this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that it happened that way. Maybe we were allowed to make a phone call, but I don't see why I would have called Ilija Koncarevic. Why would I do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And he says from that time on, he was no longer friends with you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. During his testimony, I was able to read all of his statement, and further on, he contradicts himself. He complains that I stopped calling him. He complains that I stopped all contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what day it was when you were released from jail in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the 3rd of April, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now paragraph 74. He says he was thinking about replacing Goran Hadzic because you were too much under the influence of Slobodan Milosevic and that you had come to be under his influence after these events at Plitvice. Can you tell us, is it the case that after these events at Plitvice you were indeed under the influence of Slobodan Milosevic, did you know him, did you have any communication with him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never under the direct influence of Slobodan Milosevic, although I later met him and collaborated with him. This is pure nonsense, a lie. I saw Slobodan Milosevic at a short meeting with the delegation of members of the Serbian Democratic Party from all of Croatia, and that was after the TV show about the arming of Croats, the Spegelj movie. At that time, I never talked to him, nor did I exchange any views with him. It was a large delegation, 30, maybe even 50 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember roughly when this took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been a month before Plitvice; perhaps a bit more than that. So after that -- after that TV show about Spegelj, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the year. Tell us, is it that year?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is 1991, the beginning of 1991. Because the Serbs were afraid when they heard about the arming of the Croats, and they called me from Knin, from the party, saying that Milosevic would receive a delegation in order to make us feel calmer, in a way. Because we were completely opposed idealogically to the positions taken by the then-ruling party in Serbia, the SPS. I was surprised that he wanted to receive us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what these opposed positions were? On the one hand, the SDS, and on the other side, Slobodan Milosevic and his party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, speaking in very rough terms, the SDS was an anti-Communist party with a pronounced democratic orientation. Although many of us members were former Communists. However, I and most of my friends realised what a delusion this was, this Communist delusion. And the SPS remained at least at that time in 1990, along the lines of the former League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now take a look at paragraph 78.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I might have a problem here. If I understood your question well, you asked the witness what the opposed positions were of, on the one hand, SDS, and on the other side, Slobodan Milosevic's party. And the witness gave an answer about SDS, indeed, but on the other hand, the SPS. Is that Slobodan Milosevic's party? Or is it a transcript issue? On line 21 of page 32. The witness said about the former Communists, this Communist delusion, and the SPS remained at least at that time in 1990. Is he talking about the Milosevic party there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. He -- he spoke about the difference between SDS and the SPS, but I could clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And SPS -- sorry about the fact that I'm not a hundred per cent in these acronyms. The SPS is Milosevic's party?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on to paragraph 78 now. In this paragraph, he says that he met up with you again after what had happened in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May. He says that he met you again on the 7th or 8th of May on the Vojvodina side of the Danube. Do you remember whether you met up with him after the 2nd of May on the Vojvodina bank of Danube?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember 100 per cent, but there is a high probability that that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on, he says that you were with a man who you introduced as your body-guard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not correct. Because after the well-known events of the 2nd of May, I was in Vukovar. That was the first time that I crossed the Danube, that I saved myself. There was a group of people there that I didn't know at all. They were waiting for refugees and transporting them to Serbia. I had my first body-guard, I think, in the beginning of September 1991 or the end of August. So this is ridiculous. And it's also ridiculous when he says that I had an apartment in Novi Sad, on the 7th and 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you said that you crossed the Danube then. Would you explain that? What do you mean by that? Was that the occasion when you say that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that that is that possible occasion, the only one when I was at the Danube. I fled from Vukovar on the 7th or 8th of May, crossed the Danube. As for my wife and daughter, I sent them off as refugees so that they could get that kind of accommodation, and I took a civilian car to Borovo Selo, and then I wanted to get my son in Pacetin so that I could give him a ride as well. My sister was in Pacetin too. It's not that I had an apartment in Novi Sad then. We were in Pacetin then. Again, he confused things, and he's speaking with hindsight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say whether that was the only occasion when you came to the Danube or did you come to the Danube afterwards too? I mean, after you left Croatia, after that incident in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did come, I remember, perhaps seven or eight or ten days later, once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because I see that you are linking this possible meeting with him to that particular event. Is it possible that it was some other time that you came, or is it for some other reason that you link this to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May, I was there, perhaps, two or three times, but I was a bit perplexed by what he said, the 7th or 8th of May; whereas I fled from Vukovar on the 7th or 8th of May. If it were later, then that would be more logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And at that time did you have someone standing next to you who you introduced as your body-guard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have anyone there as my body-guard. But Lazo Sarac was there that second time, when Vukasin Soskocanin drowned. I crossed the Danube only twice then, two or three times actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had intended to ask you about this later, but I see that now you -- well, you brought this up now, didn't you? So now that you've mentioned Lazo Sarac there, the second time, what were you trying to say by that, that the second time you saw Boro Savic or was it this second time that you were doing something else? Could you just clarify that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to say it honestly, the way I remember it. Because, in May, I did not have many opportunities to cross the Danube, and every time I crossed over, there was something important that happened, and I remember that. So the first time I fled from Vukovar, that was the 7th or 6th of May. I saved my life and I saved the life of my daughter, who was with me. And then around the 15th of May, I was at the Danube when Soskocanin drowned. So if Boro Savic was there, it was one of those two times. There couldn't have been a third time. I have to point out that Boro Savic was a totally unimportant person in my life. I cannot remember when it was that I would see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this Mr. Lazo Sarac who is mentioned here, whether he was ever your body-guard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, never. To put it mildly, it's ridiculous to say something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to this, to this topic, that is. This is what I'm interested in now. Let us clarify this: The text continues on the next page. It says here when Kertes took over the federal customs office, Simo Stupar from Celarevo was in charge of Goran Hadzic's security.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Simo Stupar but I know the last name Stupar from Celarevo. There's Savo. I mean, he wasn't my body-guard. Savo Stupar has a doctorate in mechanical engineering. He is ten years older than I am. He was never even armed. How could he be my body-guard?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this Mr. Savo Stupar had some kind of a job at the time? Was he employed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in Backa Palanka at a factory that manufactured agricultural equipment, but he also had some position in the Assembly of Vojvodina. I don't know exactly what was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Savo Stupar, was he or was he not your body-guard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, no, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 79, it says that you had a specific position towards Savic because he protected you. Tell me, is that correct? Did he protect you; and, if so, what did he protect you from, or who did he protect you from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I was not in jeopardy at all so that he would have to protect me. Not politically, not physically. Well, physically, certainly not. But, now, what was in his head, I cannot testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The way I understand his statement, later on, he appointed you president of the SDS Board. Well, I mean, I don't want to infer anything here, but does this correspond to the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already talked about this, and I've already said that that is not correct, that this is absolutely crazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 80, in that paragraph, he says that he noticed that you were hiding something, and he noticed that you were trying to distance yourself from him. Tell me, was there a growing distance between the two of you after those events in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear the question because I was reading this. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is the following: He noticed that you were hiding something and that you were trying to distance yourself from him. So I'm asking you now whether this did, indeed, happen after those events in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That did not happen. This has nothing to do with reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, he speaks about some pistols, 50 pistols, that you received. You were supposed to distribute them to your associates in February 1991. And he learned about this from Trifun Ivkovic. First of all, tell me, please, is it correct that you received some pistols in order to have them distributed to your associates?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. It's not only that it's not correct, it is totally insane.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand you think it is not correct, but why do you think it is insane?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, in the beginning of the war, when weapons had already arrived in Slavonia and Baranja, when the army had distributed these weapons, pistols were highly appreciated. People would give two rifles in order to get one pistol. I heard about that from various people. There weren't any pistols around. They were in very high demand. And this never happened. Nobody ever distributed pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. He says that he learned that from somebody called Trifun Ivkovic. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know Trifun very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly what you know about him.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trifun Ivkovic appeared in Eastern Slavonia as a member of an organisation known as Solidarity. I heard about them. They carried out some activities before that in Kosovo and Metohija, that same organisation Solidarity. Trifun appeared either on his own -- or, rather, always on his own and toured Serbian villages there. He did not do anything specific. According to what I know, a bit later, not much later, a bit later, he undermined our authority, the authority of us Serbs in Slavonia and Baranja. I can tell you how I learnt that if that would be of any interest to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you may. Go on.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why this story seems like a well-known cliche. Trivo Ivkovic was at a gas station in Backa Palanka, and he saw a car with the registration plates of Vukovar. He asked the driver where he was from. He learned that the guy was from Borovo Selo. He asked him: Well, how are things in Borovo Selo then? And the guy says: Well, not bad. And the guy says: Do you have money? And the other says: No, we don't. And Trivo Ivkovic then tells him: How come you don't have money? I gave a million German marks to Goran Hadzic a couple of days ago and he was supposed to distribute that money among your people in Borovo Selo. In his mind, this man cursed my mother and he thought: Well, Goran took the money for himself, the money that he was supposed to distribute. In that same second, he remembered to ask Trivo: Where did you get the million German marks from, and here you're driving this old rackety car that is worth nothing? I heard that story perhaps a month after the event, by accident. So this is the method that Trivo Ivkovic applied in order to create a rift among the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mention this name "Solidarity," was that an organisation, a political organisation, or an association?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was an association, but I don't know much about it. I only heard that Trivo Ivkovic belonged to that organisation. I did not meet any other of its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the Serbian Democratic Party did not have much contact with that organisation, or did it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not have any contact with them at all, either official or unofficial. But now I see that Boro Savic had communicated with them, but I didn't know about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 81. It says in this paragraph that until the beginning of 1991, all the contacts of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem with Belgrade went through him, exclusively through him, although he did not want to play that role. Is that correct? Are you familiar with the fact that Savic was the exclusive liaison officer with Belgrade, as it were?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that anybody had contacts with Belgrade at all, let alone that it was Boro Savic. I hear it for the first time. I believe that this is not correct, although I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If he did have contacts with Belgrade, did the Vukovar SDS Board know about those contacts? Was it informed about that communication?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never mentioned that at SDS meetings. He never spoke to me about that in private or in his official capacity at meetings. Thinking about that, I don't understand what capacity would that have been. What capacity would he have had to have in order to advocate our interests, if he was not a spy. He could not have a political role to play in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 82, he says that you spoke with the political leaders in Belgrade and that he noticed that. He says that he should go with you, but you responded that you went to Belgrade because you were fascinated by Milosevic. Did such a conversation between you and yourself [as interpreted] ever happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conversation could have only happened in Boro Savic's imagination. We never spoke about Milosevic. Belgrade was never a topic of any of our meetings at the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm interested in paragraph 166. But before that, we can -- to try tie this in with paragraph 165 which will give us a bit of a context. Please read this paragraph. My question is this: Although he never claimed that you attended that occasion but since you knew Boro Savic and you also knew Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, according to how you see things, could a conversation of this kind have ever happened between the two of them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to Boro Savic's testimony. He categorically claimed that that was on the 15th of May because he remembered that on that day Soskocanin had drowned. So this is a product of a sick mind. This is simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why do you think that this is simply impossible?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on the 15th of May, Arkan was in prison in Zagreb. Physically it was impossible. Second of all, Boro Savic was not a political factor in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. There was no need for anybody to discuss anything with him. It's just his wishful thinking about what he would have said to people if he had an opportunity. So he convinced himself that that had happened. After Plitvice, Boro Savic had to be admitted for treatment. He suffered from ill health, mental ill health. He been beaten badly at Plitvice. Before Plitvice he was a normal person, but after that, I -- I wish I could say this in private session because I really feel embarrassed when I have to say about somebody that he is insane, and I have been repeating this all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else. Perhaps my previous question was not clear enough. Since you knew Boro Savic and you also knew Raznjatovic and you knew how people treated him and vice versa, according to what you know, did Boro Savic have enough courage to address Zeljko Raznjatovic in the way he describes it here, in view of the fact that he knew who Raznjatovic was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was talking about the rally that was banned and when I said that I was on the stage on my own, that nobody dared join me, Boro was among those who didn't dare to join me. He never spoke publicly. You will remember that the Prosecution showed images from a rally, the -- when the SDS was being founded in Borovo Naselje. I spoke, and I said that the Croats have to renounce their Ustasha legacy. Boro Savic was there, and he is sitting in the last row. He is hiding behind somebody's back. He never spoke publicly or otherwise. Nobody knew about him. He did not have that kind of courage. This could not have happened, but I suppose he just got confused, and it was all in his imagination. He was delusional.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I would like to say something about the chequer-board flag. We spoke about that before the break. Boro Savic apparently had strong views about the chequer-board. Why did he not appear before 10.000 Serbs and voice his position openly? It's only with hindsight that he said it 20 years after the war, not even publicly but semi-publicly. All the deceptions, I -- I faced all of my mistakes I made, I will share with everybody publicly. I'm not trying to shun my responsibility. I'm not trying to say that I am shunning away from my political responsibility. But I will share all that with you publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave Mr. Savic aside, as well as his statement. I would like us to go back to the situation in the Serbian Democratic Party in early 1991. Could you please tell us whether there were political differences in the party when it came to the implementation of the party policies in how to approach the Croatian authorities and talk to them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were major differences. My joking comment, which was based on the facts, was that the poorer the land was, the Serbs were more extremist, whereas us Serbs in the fertile plain were more peaceful and ready to talk. The Serbs in Knin, around Knin, were radical, whereas the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia were a more peaceful and calm option. I would like to single out a person that at the beginning of the party's work was the most extremist of all, more extremist than Babic's extremism when it was at his peak. And I'm talking about Veljko Dzakula. Veljko Dzakula was the most extremist Serb that I had ever met before the developments at Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about political differences, could you please tell us whether there were any factions, any groups within the SDS? Was there any kind of polarisation? Was there an inner struggle within the party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, although it will not present the picture clearly because there was not a clear-cut division, one wing was headed by Raskovic, that was a peaceful wing, and the other was Babic's wing. Those were the two different opposing streams: Babic's on the one hand, and Raskovic's on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, briefly, what did Raskovic's faction advocate as opposed to Babic's faction?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I belonged to Raskovic's faction so I can speak on my own behalf and behalf of those people who were with me. We were in favour of negotiating with the Croats, in favour of living together, in favour of dealing with matters peacefully. And Babic accused of us of high treason. He wanted to see us hanged and arrested. They were against us. That was the gist of the matter. There were nuances, of course, but they are not important at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What did Babic's faction hold against Professor Raskovic? You told us that Professor Raskovic was the party president. What did Babic have against him, what did he hold against him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conflict escalated after Raskovic's visit to Zagreb, where he went to see Croatia's president, Mr. Tudjman. He was then attacked by all the deputies from Knin and the environs, and they called him all sorts of names. It was embarrassing to listen to that. I was at that time in Knin at the meeting of the Main Board, and Boro Savic and I did not interfere because it was their internal conflict. They were neighbours and friends who had known each other from before. It's curious from my experience that all these people who attacked Raskovic - or should I say almost everybody - who advocated war and fighting Croats, almost all of them, when the war broke out, just ran away, somewhere to western Europe; whereas we who had advocated peace and negotiations stayed in the middle of that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say Professor Raskovic had a hard time from his own people because he had talked to Tudjman. How did this meeting happen? Was it announced in advance or was it only reported later? How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember only vaguely because it was before the war and before the events at Plitvice. The Croatian side was also not quite fair in this matter.
