They did some wire-tapping and then they published the transcripts in newspapers, and then Raskovic was attacked. If the Croatian side had not done that, and Raskovic had had a chance to explain this to his own people when he came back, at their own meeting, it would have been different. I believe that's the gist of the problem. It's the same thing they tried to do to me at the negotiations in Norway, but we'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Veljko Dzakula. Can you tell us something about the incident in Pakrac? Just briefly tell us what you know about it, how well-informed you were.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have first-hand information, but I do have information that I believe is 99 per cent accurate. I heard from people, including from Boro Savic, what exactly had happened because he had closer relations with that board from Western Slavonia. Everybody was angry with Veljko Dzakula at the time because Veljko Dzakula, off his own bat, agreed with somebody in Belgrade - at least that was the story which later turned out to be not true - so he agreed with somebody in Belgrade that they attack the Croatian police somewhere in Pakrac and as soon as the shooting begins, the army would come and interpose itself between them. However, that didn't happen. Serbs started shooting. The Croatian police returned fire and arrested them, and the army never showed up. So Veljko Dzakula lied about that. That's one of the reasons why we, the delegation of the SDS from SBWS went to the president of Croatia to ask for amnesty for them, and after this incident, Veljko Dzakula reversed his policy completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before these events at Pakrac, did you know that something would happen there? How did you find out, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well. I don't remember the exact date, but I remember we had a meeting of the Executive Board on that day in a place called Dvor on the Una river. And I'm sure that not a single member of the Executive Board, which included representatives from Municipal Boards, knew that it would happen. Because I know that the representative of the party from Podravska Slatina had prepared a brief on how to promote the work of the SDS. That item was on the agenda when he was speaking. And, at that moment, I heard from people who were not members of the Executive Board, who were standing outside near the hotel where the meeting was being held, we heard from them that the Croatian police had attacked Pakrac. That came as a shock to all of us. The meeting of the Executive Board was interrupted, and Boro and I returned to Slavonia because we were expecting that roads would soon be blocked. We didn't know what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You answered a moment ago that it was over Pakrac that you met with Croatia's president, Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know it was about Pakrac. I later learned that it was about other things, too, but including Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have, please, 1D72.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in English, but I believe you had occasion to read it before in translation. If you look at the top, you will see the date, 13 March 1991. Zagreb, it's also written in the text. Is it possible that this report is precisely about that meeting you had with Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I believe it was the right date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, the people who attended this meeting were listed, the members of the delegation of the Serbian Democratic Party. You can see five names, including yours. Were these the people who attended the meeting to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there is a typo here. It says "Vojislav Vikcevic" and it should be "Vukcevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us from which constituencies, from which Municipal Boards these members of the delegation were?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojo Vukcevic was from Beli Manastir. I from Vukovar, as you know. Veljko Dzakula was from Pakrac. I believe Ilija Sasic and Dusan Ecimovic were also from Western Slavonia but I don't know exactly which boards because they were not chairmen of their boards. They were elected into the Regional Board based on their political work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I note that there is nobody from the Knin Krajina. Was there a particular reason for this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From talking to Sasic and Dzakula, as far as I was able to understand, either they hadn't dared to ask anybody or everybody refused. That's why the delegation is made up in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us to the best of your recollection what happened at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had one meeting at Tudjman's office and we were also received at the Croatian parliament where our host was Slavko Degoricija, and I remember we had certain political demands. And I learned at that meeting, in addition to what I've already described, that Dzakula was asking that those arrested in Pakrac be amnestied and that was, indeed, done. All the rest that we were promised was never done, and I can tell you later, if you wish, more about our demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, tell us. What did you ask for?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we complained. We asked that the parliament change the constitution in such a way as to make Serbs again a constituent nation as we had been for 50 years before. It was a broader political issue, and we were aware that this was a kind of maximum goal, that it was not perhaps feasible, but we did ask for something realistic and possible. And if we had received that little, the people would probably not have mobilised to wage war. The lower request was for cultural autonomy, a little bit of autonomy, although perhaps "autonomy" is too big a word. At that time, in the beginning of 1991, Serbs did not have any national iconography of their own. There were no newspapers in Cyrillic. There were no particular programmes on Croatian TV for Serbs. There would be perhaps a 30-minute TV show for Serbian people per week, or maybe a special class for Serbian children once a week, an hour per week. It now exists everywhere in the European Union. It was nothing special. I remember one of them said that Serbs, before the war, had asked for much less than we were prepared to give, but that we didn't do. We didn't do -- ask for much. We asked for the constitution, the chequer-board, and the lowest possible level of cultural autonomy. And I must admit - it would not be fair to omit this - that we were received very nicely, both by the Croatian president and the Croatian parliament. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the chequer-board emblem, what did you ask for specifically?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, among our people it was a deep-seated, accepted opinion that the chequer-board emblem, if worn on the cap of the police, for instance, is a symbol of the Ustasha state, so we asked for that emblem to be either replaced or to be modified so as to avoid the white field in the top left corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What did Tudjman reply to that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember perfectly well. I remember almost every second of that conversation. And, again, I have to be fair. Tudjman was very frank with us. He said that he has the same opinion of Ustashas as we do. At first, I thought he was not sincere, but later I realised he was. He said: Perhaps the Ustashas killed some of your ancestors during the war. They did kill my grandfather. But Tudjman says: They killed my own brother. And he said it wouldn't be a problem to accommodate us, but he has a problem with his own right wing in his own government. He didn't name any names, and I don't want to give you my interpretation of what I think he was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, when and why were you supposed to go to Obrovac for a meeting in March 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I think back about what we discussed a moment earlier, the statement of Boro Savic, when he talked about the complement of the party and the crisis in August 1990, I believe he was mistaken. The real crisis occurred in March 1991. That was the time when open confrontations broke out within the Serbian Democratic Party. In one camp were Jovan Raskovic and almost the entire board of Slavonia and Baranja and a small number of people from Knin, and in the other camp, Babic's people from Knin and the surrounding municipalities. I was quite fed up with it by that time, if not disgusted, and I was quite hesitant about whether to go to that meeting at all. Perhaps I should say why. My appointment as president of the Municipal Board in a political party, I consider that to be a democratic thing, although it was just in a political party. I thought that I should do my best. I established each and every local board. Every day I went to different villages, sometimes to two villages per day. I had meetings with people. I told them about the programme of work of the party, and I enrolled new members. Every time I went to Knin for meetings of the Main Board and later on to Pakrac when the regional committee was formed for Slavonia and Baranja, before that, I would convene a meeting of the Municipal Board in Vukovar, that is to say, a day earlier or sometimes even two or three days earlier. We would make a plan. We would adopt positions, we would vote on these positions. And I went to Knin to attend the Main Board with firm positions of the Main Board. My entire board was behind me. Immediately upon my return, on the next day or the day after that I would convene a meeting of my Municipal Board and I would bring the positions of the Main Board and we would discuss that. That's how it went. When I saw how this Main Board in Knin operated, I realised that practically all members - except for me - they present their own views only. Except for me. And they quarrelled, and it was their own personal squabbles, and so on and so forth, and I got sick of all of that and that's why I didn't feel like going there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's time for the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, Mr. Hadzic, you said that you did not want to go to attend this meeting of the SDS in Obrovac, and you explained the reasons. Can you tell us now what the reason was for you to decide to go there after all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the image here on the transcript. Can they fix this? I cannot follow that cursor, you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's very smart of you, Mr. Hadzic, to follow the cursor to know when the interpretation is finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a day or two before that meeting, I think it was two days before that meeting in Obrovac, they called me. They asked me to come to the Croatian police in Vinkovci. A friend of mine from before the war asked me to come there, and he worked at the State Security of Croatia. Ivan Zalezak [phoen] is his name. Ivan Zalezak. We hadn't seen each other in a long time because when I went into politics, we stopped all contact. And he asked me whether I would stop by and see him. I didn't know why he asked me to come. I agreed, but I did say to some of my friends that they were asking me to come and that they know where I am, so if I would not be back for a long time, they should know where I was. At that time, I was president of the SDS for Vukovar, so I thought that they should know, if I wouldn't show up in a while. Let me try to cut this short. Ivan met me in front of the Vinkovci SUP, and together with his boss, who had just been appointed, whom I had not known personally but I had heard of him because I was good friends with most of these employees there, of the State security Service in Vinkovci. His boss was Vlado Pletikosic. We went to a restaurant by the Bosut river, in town. We went for a working lunch, as they called it. I saw that the restaurant had been prepared, that it had been emptied. There weren't any other guests there, so that's where this meeting was held. The first thing they asked me, as soon as we sat down, so that we could go on talking, they asked me whether I was in favour of the war option or the peace option. Of course, I said that was in favour of the peace option. Well, they said, if you're in favour of the peace option, then are you going to go to attend the SDS meeting in Obrovac? I said that I hadn't planned to go for a variety of reasons, and I explained that a bit. I explained what the main reasons were. Of course, I did not tell them what that reason was because they really should not be interested in that. So then they asked that for their sake, in order to prevent a possible war, that I go to Obrovac to the meeting and support Professor Raskovic's stream. That was not a special problem for me because I supported that stream anyway. It wasn't any different from my own way of thinking, so I agreed to go to this meeting. And that's why I went to Obrovac. Because I had promised them that I would go and support the peace option so that war would not break out. Then I called Boro Savic, I said that we would go together, and I did not tell him that I had had this meeting because there was no need for me to tell him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us from when you knew this man called Zalezak.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew him from, say, five or six years before the war, so that would be the mid-1980s. As for this state security of theirs in Vinkovci, there were three employees there who were from Vukovar and their headquarters were in Vinkovci. So often when they would return to Vukovar they would stop by to see me in Pacetin and then we played pool there, at the local cafe. At the time, we were all members of the League of Communists because their boss -- I mean, before Pletikosic was Stipo Brajcic. Stipo Brajcic, when I was president of the youth organisation in Pacetin, he was the president of the youth organisation for the municipality of Vukovar, so I knew him from these youth activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that he was their boss before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Pletikosic, before Vlado Pletikosic, the one that I've already mentioned. Vlado Pletikosic. I also knew Darko Bekic. We were very good friends. Before all of them. He was the third person from Vukovar. Darko Bekic, not Bjekic, Bekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you went to the meeting in Obrovac. So how did this meeting go? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept my own record in my notebook. Unfortunately, the police, the Croatian police, took this away from me so I don't have it with me now. But the meeting had a few items on the agenda. I think four or five. Among other things, we were supposed to elect Dr. Vojo Vukcevic president of the Executive Board because Slavonia and Baranja were not adequately represented in the top echelons of the party. All the highest positions were in Knin. However, there was that quarrel there, precisely with regard to this option of Professor Raskovic's in favour of negotiating with Croatia and then the Babic option on the other side. I remember after the meeting, some policeman, some plain-clothes policeman. To this day, I don't know who he is, what his name is, he tried to interrogate us. A Serb policeman of the SAO Krajina. And he almost threatened us because of these political views of ours. I think that he talked to Boro Savic and Vojo Vukcevic. However, I managed to avoid them and evade that conversation. Since the meeting ended before dark, the sun was still high up, since Obrovac is close to the sea and the climate is therefore almost Mediterranean, Boro and I decided not spend the night in Obrovac. We tried to cover as many kilometres as possible in the direction of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before you go on, can I just ask you something else. Were any decisions made at that meeting? Do you remember, I mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these decisions. Something had to do with Professor Vukcevic, but I cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can go on now. I interrupted you. You were speaking about your departure from Obrovac when you went towards Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we travelled all night, we hadn't slept during the previous night, and then the meeting went on all day, we realised that we had to spend the night somewhere before Zagreb. We were planning on the Borje motel which is just before Titova Korenica. But when we got there we were taken by surprise. Although this is a big building, a big motel, they did not have any rooms. They just had a restaurant. And they said that the hotel in Plitvice is the closest to there. Since this is already a mountainous area, although it was the end of March, there was snow there. We stopped at Plitvice, had dinner there, and we went to sleep. And then, in the morning, we were awakened by automatic gun-fire and we heard this megaphone. We heard the Croatian police speaking through a megaphone: This is the Croatian state. This is the Croatian regular police. Law and order has been established. Nobody is going to have any problems, and so on. That is what I personally heard from the room while Boro Savic was taking a shower. This is a kind of tragic anecdote what he said. He -- I asked him why he was taking a shower, and he said: I want to die clean. It was Easter, both Catholic and Orthodox Easter on that day. We came down to the restaurant. There were a lot of tourists, especially Italian tourists. There were two busloads of Italian tourists there. And in the hotel there was no tell-tale signs that an incident happened. Everybody behaved normally, both waiters and tourists. Everybody had their breakfast. Boro went to the reception and inquired about the situation. When he returned, he told me that the people at the front desk told him that the road to Zagreb was passable, that the Croatian authorities had established order, and that a busload of Italian tourists had already gone to Zagreb. I said we had better stay in the hotel and see what would happen. Boro said: No, let's better leave. There's nothing for us to do here. As soon as we got in the car, it was cold. Boro took off his jacket. He drove. It was his car. I kept my short coat on, and somehow it saved me because Boro had only a shirt on, and as soon as we left in the parking, the police came from behind a house. They jumped out with automatic rifles. Obviously we got out of the car. We put our hands on the car. They came to search us. Other people came to search us while we were held at gunpoint by the first group. I had a pistol for which I had a licence to carry from the Croatian police. I had it at my belt. And one of the policemen said: This man here, he has a pistol. I said: But also I have -- I have a licence to carry it. He told me: Can I see the licence? I took out my wallet to show him the licence. However, in the wallet I also had a booklet, a membership booklet of the Serbian Democratic Party, and he saw that as well. He no longer wanted to see my licence to carry a pistol. He just shouted: Look, these are Chetniks. We have captured some Chetniks. That was before the war. Before the war even started - I'd like to emphasise that - the Serbian Democratic Party was a regular party in the Croatian parliament. They took us to the road. I was taken by surprise when I saw police vehicles, jeeps, and police officers squatting with automatic rifles, four of them, by each of the vehicles. So the action was still ongoing, it was not over as we were told at the hotel reception. When we appeared, they all rose. They lifted their rifles. They were going to beat us with rifle-butts. I was the first, and the one who was leading me told them: Don't beat them. We have to check, but it seems that they are hotel guests. The one who wanted to hit me with the rifle lowered his rifle. Boro came after me, and he didn't hear what was said before. Boro was immediately hit a metal rifle-butt and from then on, Boro was semi-conscious. He was beaten, and he no longer knew what was going on. I see when Boro had been hit, but it was only when we arrived at the police station in Karlovac did I see that his jaw was broken. I didn't realise before that -- then that he had been so heavily beaten. On the road, our hands were tied behind our backs and they ordered us to lay on the road covered with snow, and nobody had started beating us after Boro had been hit -- had been hit once. And then the man who had taken away my gun ran up to me with my pistol and he started shouting: Here's the pistol, but, look, he had fired shots from this pistol. He had fired shots. The pistol is still dirty. My -- my pistol was never fired, but I had kept it around my belt for such a long time that it got dirty from the woollen clothes. And as I was lying down, he used my pistol to hit me in my head and he broke my skull in two places. He hit me as hard as he could. He also kicked me in his boot shot leg [as interpreted]. In karate, this kick is called yoko-geri-kekomi. He hit me in the left kidney and injured it. After that, I peed blood for two months. And then an ambulance arrived and a vehicle with a Croatian TV crew arrived. I recognised a man, he was either a doctor or a paramedic from Vukovar. I was happy to see him because I thought that he would explain the misunderstanding. He, however, looked at me with spite in his eyes. He almost spat at me. The TV crew came with a camera and then the police came with the -- the key for the handcuffs. They unlocked the handcuffs, and then just for the camera, they went over the whole procedure again. They told us: Hands up, and they arrested us again for the TV. When the TV crew recorded that, they left, and then they tied our hands behind our backs again and they started beating us, but they were not hitting us with rifles or any other implements. They just kicked us and beat us with their hands. They continued doing that for some ten minutes or so, and all that time, we were shouting: People, we are hotel guests. They did not pay heed to that. And then one of them - probably their boss - said: Ah, you're hotel guests. We're going to return you to the hotel. That was a mistake because they took us to another group, to barricades, some kilometre or 2 kilometres away from that place. There were about 30 or 40 police officers there. And now the second group didn't know anything about that being a possible mistake. They thought this we must be Chetniks and must be guilty of a crime. So we were handed over by the first group to the second group, and the latter group continued beating us. All that time our hands were tied behind our backs. And then they took us to the third barricade in a police vehicle, in a Puch jeep. Boro and I were sitting in the back and there were two police officers in front of us and there were two police officers on each of our sides. Then one of them took my chin in his hands. He took a knife and said: Now I'm going to slit his throat. And then the co-driver said: Don't slit his throat now. There'll be blood all over the upholstery in the car. Wait until we stop. I started praying to God that we never stop because I really thought that they would slit my throat. And when we stopped, I realised that we stopped by a third barricade where -- manned by some 20 or 30 police officers, so I thought maybe they wouldn't slit my throat in front of them. Then they threw us out of the car and they said to the third group: Here they are. You do whatever you want with them. And the third group also beat us, continued beating us. Our hands were tied all that time. When all that was over, the third round of beating, that is, they forced us to get into a police van without any seats. There was just a floor. And then two police officers entered. They did not wear camouflage uniforms, but, rather, blue, regular police uniforms. They had two huge batons, the kind that I'd never seen before. Boro and I were still tied and there were two men, and these two men were beating us for some ten minutes in that vehicle, from head to toe. They injured my leg muscle so badly that I couldn't stand without cramps. I still get cramps in my both legs when I stand longer. And that was the end of the physical ill-treatment. Then they transferred us to another vehicle, a Citroen van, similar to the previous one, and they took us into a forest. They undressed us. They opened the windows. We were almost naked. And they told us: If there are shots we'll come and shoot you, so don't move. We were there in the vehicle, and the Croatian civilians who lived there came up to us and they -- they were saying: Let us gouge his eyes and I will sell them and make money on that. I was afraid all the time that somebody would really come and slit my throat or torture me. And then they took us to the police station in Karlovac, and that's when the ill-treatment finally stopped. While they were beating us, at first I thought I could reason with them and that I could explain. I was shouting: People, we're not guilty of anything. I just went to see Tudjman as a member of a delegation in Zagreb. I thought that that would help. And one of them said: If Tudjman received you, he will be beaten too. So it was funny and sad at the same time. And I would like to say one more thing. While I was being beaten, all that time I didn't feel any pain. I suppose that my adrenaline was very high, and I only started feeling pain when all the beating stopped. I suppose that I was afraid for my own life, and that was the first time that I was ever hit or beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived Karlovac and later, did anybody tell you why things were done to you? Were you interrogated? Did somebody explain to you why you had been brought in?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, the physical ill-treatment stopped in Karlovac. There were public security inspectors there who received us. They offered us water. I don't drink coffee but Boro may have been offered some coffee. And they told us that that was a misunderstanding, a mistake. They apologised. And we thought that they really meant it. Boro and I even suggested that they should take us back so that he could take his car. It was a Golf car, relatively new. It was worth a lot of money. At that time it was very hard to buy a Golf car like that. And they said: Don't worry, we will bring the car over. And we believed them. And then we had an interview with two State Security Service inspectors. They also apologised to us and they told us that we would be released. However, something happened. I don't know what. Only later did I realise that a political decision had been reached, and that we were to be put together with the others who had been arrested. I didn't know at that time that some 15 other Serbs from Plitvice had been arrested at the same time. Of us 15 or 16, only one wore a Krajina police uniform. Only one of them was a participant in the events. All the rest were civilians. Most of them were in slippers and it was snowing, which means that all these people had been arrested in their homes. They had all been badly beaten. When I saw one of them, his mouth, his left side of his mouth, and it was funny and sad at the same time when I saw him -- when I saw him, and they kept us all in -- in a gym and later that evening we were taken to Zagreb. First to the prison hospital. I was examined by a doctor, actually, all of us were. I was the last one to be checked. The rest left, and the duty officer who had brought us in asked the doctor: How many have to stay in the hospital and how many will go to the prison in Simunska Street? It was only then that I realised, when I heard him say that and when I heard the doctor's response, what my position was. The Dr. told him: Are you normal? They are not even for the hospital, they are for a morgue. And all the 15 or 16 of them have to be hospitalised and assisted by doctors. That's how badly they are all beaten. So we were taken to various hospital rooms. We -- we were not allowed to share, any of us, the same room although I only knew Boro, nobody else. The following day, Degoricija came to visit us. He greeted us, even kissed us as if we were the closest of kins. And he told us that that was nothing more but a tragic mistake. After that, on the following day, on the way to the toilet, a patient from another room who was free to walk around gave me a newspaper article to read. When I was in the toilet, I read the newspaper article and I believe that the newspaper was Vjesnik. After having visited us, Degoricija gave a statement and said: I visited Hadzic in the hospital. He was crying on my shoulder and he admitted that he had opened fire on Croats and he is sorry. This was even worse than any of the beating and the fear that I would be killed because I realised that that was the end of the world, that there was nobody I could talk to and explain things to, that there was no institution that I could go to, to explain things. And then the next day, Boljkovac and Degoricija came. They said that Boro and I should write statements, separate statements, and they would release us. We got ready. We packed. I went to the same admission room where I had left my things, and I saw a newspaper on the desk of the policeman on duty and a large headline said: Chetnik hordes from Serbia came to Borovo Selo. And then I concluded that they were releasing me not because they really wanted to but because something was going on there that didn't suit them. So we went in two cars to Vukovar, Boljkovac and Degoricija were in the car ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know, did you get any notification in the days following that meeting that there was any fighting around?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no fighting. We didn't hear about anything. If there was any talk, it was in the other camp. We, in the Raskovic camp, didn't know anything about it. When we arrived at Plitvice after dinner, our waiter approached us, saying that there was talk about the Croatian police possibly coming to Plitvice, but I didn't think I had anything to be afraid of. There was Croatian police in Zagreb as well. Why shouldn't they be in Plitvice? I had no reason to fear them. But I remember the waiter said: They're not crazy after all, you know, it's Easter for them too. They would not make trouble on Easter day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with that pistol that you had, the licence to carry a fire-arm, all the documents that you had on you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my documents were stolen. When I say "stolen," they just took them away from me, but it was pure theft because only the regular police had to do -- only the regular police had the right to do that. So they took everything I had, including some cheques that I was supposed -- for costs that I was hoping to get reimbursement for from -- from the SDS, and I was thinking that maybe if I get to Zagreb, they would be returned to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you again enumerate all the documents that were taken away from you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My ID and my driving licence that was in my wallet and the SDS membership booklet and all the documents I had in my wallet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say a few days later they took you back. They took you back in their own vehicle.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a car of the State Security of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Savic got back his Volkswagen Golf?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They returned it to him later, but it was shot at. It had holes from rifle bullets. That was done on purpose. But they did not pay him any damages, as far as I know. Although, after this, I don't believe a single word he says. But he said at the time that he never received any damages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where exactly did they take you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They drove us to the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar. We didn't even know at the time that the -- the Assembly was in permanent session and they didn't want to disband until we show up. I wanted to go up, but Degoricija said: No need. Go and have some rest. What he actually didn't want to happen is that people should see us with the traces of beating on our faces. In the hospital, we received some treatment but it was still visible. But then you a saw a group of my former schoolmates, Croats, who were standing on the other side of the street, across from the Assembly. I was just feeling happy I was alive at that moment and I waved at them in greeting, but nobody responded. I learned later they had come to protest against the fact that we were released. I still wonder do they really think, did they really think, that we should go to prison? Because at that time we were completely innocent. We had done nothing wrong. Anyway, soon afterwards, I learned why they were standing there. And I also learned later they were members of the HDZ, but that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After your release from jail, can you remember, did you continue with your political activity as a member of the Assembly of Vukovar, for instance?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued with what I believed was normal activity at the time. I was not even aware of my real physical and mental condition. Only later when I saw medical reports, including the findings of a psychiatrist I had spoken to, I realised I was in big trouble. But the very first evening after being released, I went to Borovo Selo. We held a meeting there, and I said: We don't need roadblocks anymore, now that Boro and I were released. That was maybe on the following day, but I believe it was the same evening. In those other villages, the roadblocks or barricades were removed immediately, and in Borovo Selo on the next day, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me, how did you find out about roadblocks in the first place? Did you go to Borovo Selo or did you go to your own home and call them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in that car of the MUP of Croatia, we were unable to go through Brsadin village, which is a Serbian village, but people recognised me. I told them to remove the barricades. My village is on a side road, not the main road, and I saw the barricades and the roadblocks, and I couldn't fathom why this was happening. I thought it was all leading to a conflict that was completely unnecessary, and I thought that neither Boro Savic nor I had done anything over which people should go into a conflict, so I continued with my normal work the very following day. I cannot now say with exact chronology what happened when, whether it was on the first, second, or third day, but at any rate, the roadblocks were removed in Borovo Selo after we were released. And I believe Veljko Dzakula and Ilija Sasic were there in Borovo Selo too. Although I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you told people in Borovo Selo that they should remove the roadblocks, was it your own decision, something that you arrived at on your own, or was it a demand put to you by the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barricades had been set up because of me, practically. And I thought that since I had come back, they were no longer needed, but that was also in keeping with the agreement I made before travelling to Obrovac that we should work to normalise the relations between Serbs and Croats. And generally speaking, I have always been against barricades. And those later barricades that were set up because of the attacks at Borovo Selo in August, it was Degoricija who asked me to remove them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not "attacks at Borovo Selo in August." It is attacks in Borovo Selo with a type of mortar called Armbrust, A-r-m-b-r-u-s-t. [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you got into touch with people from Borovo Selo after you were released, did they tell you what had happened while you were in jail? Was there any unrest or something like that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me everything, but I can't really recall it all now because I was still in a state of shock after the beatings. I know Vukasin Soskocanin was in negotiations with the Croatian police, with Zagreb, demanding our release.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1778.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see in this report that the Serbian National Council - I'm translating it differently than the translation we have. The translation says "Serbian National Alliance" but it is the original that is authoritative - called upon the Serbian people to refrain from any action. Look through the text, please, and then we'll discuss it. [In English] In English, it is under title: "Serbs in Borovo region form police force." Is on the very bottom of the left side of the screen. [Interpretation] My question is: Were you told that during your absence while you were in prison about those 25 policemen who walked out of their service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard then that 25 policemen had left the force, but I didn't know at that time that it was connected to the incident and our arrest at Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After this event -- after this event, did you go to Zagreb for any purpose?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of times I spoke to Mr. Degoricija on the phone. I was on good terms with him. By that time, he was already chief of the State Security of Croatia. In fact, assistant minister for the State Security. I complained that I did not have any documents, that they had taken money and documents away from me, everything. And he said by way of a joke: Why are you complaining? I also said that I don't have a pistol either. And he said: What do you need a pistol for? If you need it, we're going to give you a rifle. That's what he told me on the phone, by way of a joke, of course. And I didn't find that very funny. I asked him to try to find my things, and he called me about ten or 15 days later and told me to come to Zagreb so that they could see what could be done, so that they could return this to me. Since I had no documents at the time, I did not try to get new ones. I thought that they would return them to me. I borrowed a car from a friend from Vukovar and I asked my best friend to come along with me to Zagreb. And he had documents so that if the police would stop us, then -- since I did my military service in Zagreb in the JNA, I knew Zagreb well. We went to the MUP directly to see Boljkovac. He received me immediately, jumping the queue. Degoricija was waiting there as well, and we started this comradely, friendly meeting, as if there were no problems whatsoever. I said: Give me my money and my documents. And they said: Oh, never mind that now. If you can, try to speak to Milan Babic and see whether he would remove barricades from the railroad so that we could have trains running through Knin. Although they were aware of the relations within the SDS, I explained to them that Babic was completely independent and that his political option was my complete opposite and he would not really listen to what I had to say, but I did promise to call him and tell him that. They said that it's not smart for us to quarrel, that I should influence Boro Savic, that Boro and I should withdraw the charges that we brought against Tudjman because of the mistreatment we had suffered in Plitvice on the hands of the Croatian police. I said that on my own behalf I would withdraw these charges but I don't know, I cannot guarantee that Boro Savic would also drop his charges. And they said: All right. Now go to the centre of Zagreb, Zrinjevac, the prosecutor's office. They gave me the name of some prosecutor - I've forgotten it by now - and report to him and he'll give you your things back. I went there and this man returned only six bullets, the ones that I had in the pocket of my jacket. Nobody had searched me. These were reserve bullets for my pistol, and I didn't really need that. He said that the people who took away my documents and my pistol hid all of that because they want to keep it as a trophy, and therefore they cannot find any of it. And after that, I just went back to Pacetin. After that, Degoricija continued to call me practically every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what kind of charges did they want you and Boro Savic to drop?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Boro Savic and I, a few days after our return from Zagreb, went to Belgrade. I went to the American embassy. I had a meeting there. But before that, I went to see a group of lawyers together with him and they agreed to represent us for free in our complaint against Tudjman and the Croatian state. Savo Andjelkovic and Mitar Lazovic were their names. Lazovic was old even at that time. He was old even then. We, or at least I at least, all the documents I had, the medical findings, actually, not the documents. Medical findings. That's what I handed over to the lawyers, and I don't have that now. But it doesn't really matter, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you were asked to come to Zagreb after the visit with these lawyers. Or, actually, probably after charges were filed.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 15th of April. As soon as they found out that we had filed charges, they said that that was not politically proper, what is Tudjman to be blamed for. At that time, we did not know about this notion of command responsibility, what I am here for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said after this contact with Boljkovac and Tudjman, there were some other contacts too. I mean, well, actually, now, were there any contacts, and, if so, can you tell us with who from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from Degoricija there was constant contact. So primarily with Degoricija. Maybe there were others, but I cannot recall right now. I continued my contacts with the Croats in the municipality of Vukovar as well. In a way, well, perhaps it is inconceivable for me to say that now, but I personally had good relations with the Croats in the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now in relation to these contacts with Degoricija, did he ask you for something, in the sense of certain activity, political activities, that should be carried out?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't have to ask me for that because I supported the same thing then, that barricades were not needed. There's no reason for us to wage war. Officially what he asked for, and I've already said that, was to have the barricades removed, the ones that were set up in Borovo Selo yet again but for a different reason. I remember that. Because he was in constant contact with us and the members of the Regional Board of the SDS from Western Slavonia, Sasic and Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember perhaps in that period, in April 1991 -- well, you said that there were contacts with people in the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar. Do you remember whether any measures were taken there, in order to calm down the situation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot get this in the right chronological order now but Degoricija often came to Vukovar and had meetings, both with us and joint meetings. We called this co-ordination of all political parties in the municipality of Vukovar. And I think at that moment both Boljkovac and Degoricija were attending a meeting in the municipality of Vukovar, so this could have been April. But this meeting -- well, at least -- for at least while I was there, that was a meeting with the Serbs, but I think that before that they had a meeting with their own party. I remember that Rade Leskovac was in that meeting and I remember some parallel of his, or, rather, a digression when he said -- I'm going to paraphrase now. It would be strange for someone to walk around town without any clothes on, but people should wonder why it is that way. It wouldn't be surprising if everybody did that. It had to do with the problem of the Serbs, and I remember that he wanted to draw this parallel, and that's how I remember that he attended the meeting too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D2191.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of the conclusions of the Presidency of the municipality of Vukovar on the 10th of April, 1991. Since you were a member of the Assembly of the municipality of Vukovar at the time, please do read this conclusion and let us see whether you remember when it was adopted, this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and I see the date, the 10th of April. Although it's a specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the following: It says here that this decision was made by the Presidency of the municipality of Vukovar. Who made up this Presidency? What did that mean, "the Presidency of the municipality of Vukovar"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm a bit confused by this because, according to the statute of the municipality, I think that that did not exist but I'm not sure. It could be some political group, something like that, of members of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present when this decision was being made, or did you know about this decision at all, that it had been reached?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember now with any precision, so I don't want to be involved in any kind of guess-work. I think it was when Boljkovac and Degoricija were there, and, in a way, this would be acceptable, invoking the peace option, if I saw all of this right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 is characteristic, where it says: "We call upon all citizens, political parties and institutions of the system to refrain from any activity that might aggravate what is already an extremely difficult situation."

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, what you read out is paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2. Yes, I was reading out number 2 and I see that there is something similar in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The essence of my question is whether you remember that the municipality of Vukovar, regardless of whether it's the Assembly itself or the Presidency or the president or anybody else, sent this kind of appeal to anyone?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that in the month of April the Assembly met - the full Assembly, that is - so it's the Presidency that had to decide because the entire Assembly could not meet. So I think it wasn't the Assembly. As for this notion of the Presidency, well, I'm not sure. This is basically the first time I'm coming across this. It did not exist in the political work of the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see paragraph 4 of this document. I see that all citizens of the municipality of Vukovar are being called upon to mark the anniversary of the liberation of Vukovar on the 12th of April in a solemn way. Do you remember whether any such thing did take place on that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in vain. It certainly didn't happen. That was the day of the liberation of Vukovar from fascism. By then it was not really being celebrated, in particular. It was celebrated in Tito's day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a new document, so -- I see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break. Resume on Monday at 9.00. Mr. Hadzic, you know the drill, I suppose, about discussing your testimony with other people, which is not allowed, and you know our decision about contact with your Defence and, of course, you can't have contact with OTP. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of July, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.58 p.m.,
